subject: math
cluster: Visualize relationships between two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects
description: Students move fluently between two dimensions and three dimensions in two directions. First, given a three-dimensional solid (cube, rectangular prism, triangular or other prism, cylinder, cone, pyramid, or sphere) and a cutting plane, they identify the shape of the two-dimensional cross-section that the plane produces, and they describe how that shape changes as the plane moves or tilts (for example, a plane parallel to a cylinder's base gives a circle, while a plane perpendicular to the base and through the axis gives a rectangle, and an oblique plane gives an ellipse). Second, given a two-dimensional region rotated $360^\circ$ about a line (an axis of revolution), they identify the solid of revolution that is generated (for example, a rectangle rotated about one side sweeps out a cylinder, a right triangle rotated about a leg sweeps out a cone, and a semicircle rotated about its diameter sweeps out a sphere). They reason about which axis produces which solid, predict the radius and height of the resulting solid from the dimensions of the flat region, and use these relationships to solve measurement problems such as finding the volume or surface area of the generated solid. The highest expectation is to justify why a given plane or rotation yields a particular figure by appealing to the symmetry and structure of the solid, and to handle cases where the axis is offset from the region (producing a washer or torus-like solid) or where the cutting plane passes through edges and vertices.
subSkills: Identify the cross-section formed when a plane cuts a cube or rectangular prism (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, or hexagon depending on the plane's orientation)
Identify the cross-section of a cylinder for planes parallel to the base (circle), perpendicular through the axis (rectangle), and oblique (ellipse)

Identify the cross-section of a cone for planes parallel to the base (circle), through the apex perpendicular to the base (isosceles triangle), and oblique (ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola as conic sections)

Identify the cross-section of a pyramid (the base shape scaled down for a plane parallel to the base; a triangle through the apex) and of a sphere (always a circle, largest as a great circle through the center)
Describe how a cross-section's shape and size change as the cutting plane is translated or tilted

Identify the solid of revolution generated when a two-dimensional region is rotated $360^\circ$ about a given axis (rectangle about a side gives a cylinder; right triangle about a leg gives a cone; semicircle about its diameter gives a sphere)
Determine the radius and height (or other key dimensions) of a solid of revolution from the dimensions and placement of the rotated region
Recognize when an axis offset from the region produces a hollow solid (washer or ring) and describe the resulting cross-section through the axis
Apply cross-section and rotation reasoning to compute a measurement (volume or surface area) of the generated solid

problemArchetypes.name: Cross-section of a cylinder
problemArchetypes.example: A plane cuts a right circular cylinder so that the plane is parallel to the cylinder's circular base. What is the shape of the cross-section? Answer: a circle. (A plane through the axis perpendicular to the base instead gives a rectangle, and an oblique plane gives an ellipse.)

problemArchetypes.name: Cross-section of a cone
problemArchetypes.example: A right circular cone is cut by a plane that passes through the apex and is perpendicular to the base. What is the shape of the cross-section? Answer: an isosceles triangle. (A plane parallel to the base gives a circle; a slanted plane not through the apex gives an ellipse.)

problemArchetypes.name: Cross-section of a cube or prism
problemArchetypes.example: A cube of edge length $6$ is sliced by a plane perpendicular to one face and parallel to an edge. What is the shape and area of the cross-section? Answer: a $6\times 6$ square with area $36$ square units. (A plane through three non-adjacent faces can instead give a triangle, and a plane cutting all six faces can give a hexagon.)

problemArchetypes.name: Solid generated by rotating a region
problemArchetypes.example: A rectangle with width $3$ and height $5$ is rotated $360^\circ$ about its height (the side of length $5$). What solid is generated and what are its dimensions? Answer: a cylinder with radius $3$ and height $5$, so its volume is $V=\pi r^2 h=\pi(3)^2(5)=45\pi$ cubic units.

problemArchetypes.name: Cone or sphere from rotation
problemArchetypes.example: A right triangle with legs $4$ (horizontal) and $9$ (vertical) is rotated $360^\circ$ about the vertical leg. What solid results, and what is its volume? Answer: a cone with radius $4$ and height $9$, so $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h=\frac{1}{3}\pi(4)^2(9)=48\pi$ cubic units. (A semicircle of radius $r$ rotated about its diameter instead gives a sphere of volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Offset axis producing a hollow solid
problemArchetypes.example: A square of side $2$ is rotated $360^\circ$ about a vertical line that is $3$ units to the left of the square's nearest side. Describe the solid generated. Answer: a hollow cylindrical ring (washer) with inner radius $3$ and outer radius $5$, height $2$; its volume is $\pi(R^2-r^2)h=\pi(5^2-3^2)(2)=\pi(25-9)(2)=32\pi$ cubic units.

Easy.description: A single direct identification with a familiar solid and a plane or axis in standard position. The student names the cross-section shape or the solid of revolution with no computation, choosing from the canonical cases (parallel-to-base, through-the-axis). This is where a tier1 worksheet starts and most of its items live.
constraints: Solid is a cylinder, cone, cube, rectangular prism, or sphere in standard orientation
The cutting plane is parallel or perpendicular to a base/face, or the axis of rotation is a side of the region
Answer is the name of one shape (circle, rectangle, square, triangle) or one solid (cylinder, cone, sphere); no numeric work required
The defining relationship is the standard one (plane parallel to base of a cylinder gives a circle; rectangle rotated about a side gives a cylinder)

Medium.description: Identification combined with one quantitative step, or a less standard plane or axis. The student must determine a dimension (radius, height, side count, or area) or handle an oblique plane, a pyramid, or a plane through a vertex. This band is the upper end of tier1 and the lower end of tier2.
constraints: May involve an oblique plane (ellipse), a plane through an apex, or a plane producing a triangle, pentagon, or hexagon from a cube
Requires reading off the radius and height of a generated solid from the region's dimensions, or computing the area of a simple cross-section
May ask for the volume or surface area of the generated solid using $V=\pi r^2 h$, $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$, or $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with exact answers in terms of $\pi$
Requires choosing the correct axis or plane orientation among two or three plausible options

Hard.description: A multi-step problem that chains identification, dimensional reasoning, and measurement, or that involves an offset axis, a conic-section cross-section, or a justification of why a figure results. The student must build the solid mentally, extract every needed dimension, and complete a computation or argument. This is where a tier2 worksheet ends.
constraints: Offset axis of revolution producing a washer/ring, requiring inner and outer radii and a difference $\pi(R^2-r^2)h$
Conic-section cross-sections of a cone (circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) classified by the plane's angle relative to the slant
Combines two ideas, e.g. identify the solid generated by a rotation and then compute its volume or surface area, with exact values in radicals or $\pi$
Requires a justification: explain, using the solid's symmetry, why the plane or rotation yields the named figure, or determine which axis yields a target solid

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes every cross-section of a cylinder is a circle, ignoring the orientation of the cutting plane
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a plane through the cylinder's axis perpendicular to the base, answers 'circle' instead of the correct rectangle

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the solid of revolution with the flat region itself, naming the two-dimensional shape rather than the solid
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States that rotating a rectangle about a side produces a 'rectangle' or a 'square' instead of a cylinder

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student rotates the region about the wrong axis or swaps the radius and height, so the dimensions of the generated solid are interchanged
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a $3\times 5$ rectangle rotated about its side of length $5$, gives a cylinder with radius $5$ and height $3$ (volume $75\pi$) instead of radius $3$, height $5$ (volume $45\pi$)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student forgets the $\frac{1}{3}$ factor and treats a cone of revolution as if it were a cylinder when computing volume
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a right triangle with legs $4$ and $9$ rotated about the leg of length $9$, gives $V=\pi(4)^2(9)=144\pi$ instead of $\frac{1}{3}\pi(4)^2(9)=48\pi$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes a sphere can have a non-circular cross-section, such as an ellipse or oval, when cut by a tilted plane
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims an oblique plane through a sphere produces an ellipse instead of a circle (every plane cross-section of a sphere is a circle)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores an offset axis and treats the rotation as if the axis passed through the region, producing a solid cylinder instead of a hollow ring
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a $2\times 2$ square rotated about a line $3$ units away, gives a solid cylinder of radius $2$ (volume $8\pi$) instead of a washer with inner radius $3$, outer radius $5$ (volume $32\pi$)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misidentifies the cross-section of a cone for an oblique plane, assuming it must be a triangle or a circle rather than a conic such as an ellipse
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a plane cutting a cone at an angle through both slant sides without passing through the apex, answers 'triangle' instead of the correct ellipse

_comment_itemCounts: Single ramped worksheet covers this standard well; tier1/tier2 counts are provided per default in case a two-sheet split is used. Lesson 5+5, worksheet single/tier1/tier2 = 15 each, quiz 8.
